segments.original: Although American independent cinema enjoyed one of its great moments in the 1980s and 1990s, it was by no means a phenomenon confined to that period. True independent cinema - produced outside the major studios - is nothing new in the United States. Small studios and lone filmmakers have been making their own productions since the earliest days of cinema.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Rather than being defined simply by production and distribution criteria, indie cinema is, at least in theory, cinema with ideas of its own, resistant to the norms of the mainstream and loosely tied to the counterculture. American independent films are seen as the creations of filmmakers with distinctive points of view, who usually produce and retain the rights to their work. This tradition includes names as varied as Andy Warhol (1929-1989), Robert Altman (1925-2006), John Cassavetes (1929-1987), and George A. Romero (b. 1940).

segments.original: From whatever angle one chooses to analyze Pulp Fiction, the conclusion is inescapable that it was not only one of the most important films of the '90s but also a major influence on an entire generation, a cinematic watershed, so to speak. The unmistakable filmmaking style that Quentin Tarantino had so firmly established with his Reservoir Dogs just two years earlier, blending varied techniques into a unique and original result, reached a kind of early climax with Pulp Fiction, since renowned filmmakers usually have a significant growth curve, which can last decades, before reaching their peak. And I would not even dare to state categorically, after all these years, that Tarantino's second feature really is his high point, because I honestly could no longer say; however, without a shadow of a doubt, this is the film that threw the doors wide open for the director and that also seeped most deeply, immediately, and indelibly into pop culture, with a veritable avalanche of iconic dialogue, unforgettable songs, and breathtaking sequences.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: But what makes Pulp Fiction Pulp Fiction? That is a question that can have a myriad of answers, all of them valid. In my view, however, the work's great highlight is the way Tarantino, who wrote the screenplay based on stories created by himself and Roger Avary (b. 1965), tells three largely independent stories - four, if we count the one about the couple trying to steal some money, which opens and closes the film - inspired by the kind of literature the title openly announces, in a complex nonlinear narrative structure, each with its own beginning, middle, and end, but all in dialogue with one another within the overall theme of the criminal underworld in and around Los Angeles.

segments.original: It is easy to spot films that were influenced by Pulp, such as Memento and City of God. The transformation - or, perhaps, appropriation - of nonlinear narrative as something of his own is, I would say, one of Tarantino's most misunderstood traits. The director is accused of being a copycat, a plagiarist, and every synonym for it, as if no other director did the same, or as if Tarantino himself had not stated that he uses references to works he likes to a greater or lesser degree. But what the director knows how to do is turn everything he "copies or borrows" into something easily identifiable as his own. We know we are watching a Tarantino film even if we come to it halfway through. The same can be said of directors such as Woody Allen and Steven Spielberg. Whether that is a good or bad thing is not for us to judge here. What is clear is that Tarantino knows how to turn what is seemingly commonplace into his signature, and that is what he did with nonlinear narrative in Pulp Fiction: he transformed the basics into a structure that unfolds into several parallel and sometimes tangential stories which, in the end, make plain the director's command of the camera and of editing, not to mention the ever-present and always perfect soundtrack, another cinematic watershed, by the way.

segments.original: Each of the narrative threads that populate Tarantino's episodic film is riddled with dialogue that works as an expansion of what we saw in his first film. While his first film had dialogue confined to a single circle of people made up of white gangsters or bank robbers, in Pulp Fiction we see a mix of different characters in a pair dynamic (or nearly so): the couple of amateur robbers who open and close the film (Tim Roth and Amanda Plummer); the hitman duo Vincent Vega (John Travolta, revived by Tarantino) and Jules Winnfield (Samuel L. Jackson, revealed to the world here) on a mission; crime boss Marsellus Wallace (Ving Rhames) and Butch (Willis), a boxer in the twilight of his career, running into the rapists Zed (Peter Greene) and Maynard (Duane Whitaker); Vincent Vega and Mia Wallace (Uma Thurman) grappling with a heroin overdose and with drug dealer Lance (Eric Stoltz) and his wife Jody (Rosanna Arquette); and Vincent, Jules, Jimmie (Tarantino himself), and "problem solver" Mr. Wolf (Harvey Keitel) dealing with an unpleasant situation involving blood and bits of brain splattered all over a car.

segments.original: Each line of dialogue is carefully crafted to fit its character and that character's interaction with the other. There is a bit of everything, plus Tarantino's incredible ability to slip in pop culture references at every turn. The lines about the little differences between Europe and the United States, about Marsellus getting "medieval" on Zed, about the Bible passage Jules quotes before killing, and many others are, if we like, as empty of content as they are full of rhythm; or as full of social criticism as we choose to imagine, without forgetting that several of them are lifted - some word for word - from earlier works, in yet another demonstration of Tarantino's ability to remix what already exists and make it his own.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: One of the specialties of brothers and partners Joel and Ethan Coen is twisting well-established Hollywood genres into delightful, exuberant contemporary forms. The films of this duo, two of the most important filmmakers to emerge in the United States in the 1980s, remain excellent, and the fiendishly clever Fargo ranks among the best. It is a sordid tale that draws gasps of admiration and shock, but also big laughs. On screen are embezzlement, kidnapping, deceptions, misunderstandings, and murder, as well as another constant in the Coens' films: a crime that spins completely out of control.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The Coens' clever ideas yield a peculiar, bizarre tragicomedy that manages to be both hugely entertaining and violently disturbing, through impeccably executed twists that contrast the essential effectiveness and innocence of some characters with the depravity of others. The hapless criminals and their victims are not there to elicit empathy, but to be cruelly manipulated for our amusement. The cold, malevolent spirit that has resurfaced in many of their other films led one critic of their work to call them "artsy annoyances." But that does not diminish their flagrant talent for astonishing, bewildering, and entertaining audiences. Despite its stark look, Fargo is one of the brothers' most tender works, full of signature sequences and running gags that stretch across several scenes, but also with the redemptive comfort of plain decency. McDormand and the Coens' screenplay won two Oscars for breaking the old rules in a one-of-a-kind murder case.

Gattaca, from nineteen ninety-seven, Donnie Darko, from two thousand one, and A Scanner Darkly, from two thousand six, are independent productions reminiscent of the intimate science fiction of Alphaville, from nineteen sixty-five, by Jean-Luc [[pron: Godard|Go-dar]] (born in nineteen thirty).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: A group of independent production companies came to dominate the circuit, among them October Films, Good Machine, and the once-mighty Miramax. However, since many lesser, mainstream-oriented films also benefited from the scene's prestige, over time the "indie spirit" became more of a label than a true ethic. Some of the major studios created supposedly autonomous subsidiaries, such as Fox Searchlight Pictures, aiming to capture some of the indie spirit under their own roofs.

segments.original: Many filmmakers take a "one for them, one for me" approach, alternating between a film made at the studio's behest and one seasoned with their own idiosyncrasies. With the Hellboy films (2004-2008) sandwiching Pan's Labyrinth (2006), Mexican director Guillermo del Toro (b. 1964) was able to explore a Spanish-language story closer to his heart while also producing more commercial adventures drawn from comic books.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: What sets winners apart from losers? Victories from defeats? What would truly allow a person to avoid failure and be driven to win? And what is the point of this relentless pursuit of winning, in its most normative sense? Just to win? To win for whom? For others? For the world? For oneself? That is how the first feature film by Jonathan Dayton and Valerie Faris premiered at the 2006 Sundance Film Festival, opening on Richard Hoover (Greg Kinnear) giving a talk about his self-help book introducing the nine steps needed to become a winner. Hoover's world is thus divided into two opposing positions: either you win, or you fail. The weight of the family, however, is carried by Sheryl (Toni Collette), wife, mother and the household's main breadwinner. Richard, meanwhile, although he applies the ideas in his book to raising his children, is frustrated at being unable to sell it to any publisher. In the figure of Sheryl's brother, Frank Ginsberg (Steve Carell), a scholar of the writer Proust, lies the tragic theme of the man who failed to kill himself. Forced to stay with his sister's family, Frank is reintroduced to his nephew Dwayne (Paul Dano), who, driven by his desire to become a test pilot, has taken a vow of silence, also as a result of his interest in the writings of Friedrich Nietzsche. But there are still more members of this captivating, relatable family to meet.

tracks.title: Learn more: Little Miss Sunshine: Beyond Appearances (2)

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Besides those already mentioned, the heart of the story also includes Edwin Hoover (Alan Arkin), Richard's father. Kicked out of a retirement home over problems with heroin, this old man ends up developing his more human side in the bond he nurtures with Olive (Abigail Breslin), the couple's daughter, who sees in her grandfather the coach responsible for keeping alive her aspiring dreams of becoming Little Miss Sunshine. When the family learns that Olive has unexpectedly qualified to compete for the title, they all set off on a trip to Redondo Beach, crammed into a charming – and rusty – yellow Volkswagen bus. Michael Arndt's screenplay then throws the viewer into a far-from-conventional journey. The road trip formula is unquestionably successful when it carries a deep study of the idea of family, both as a whole and in its individuality. On the other hand, there are some questionable aspects to Arndt's work. The most tragic circumstances, which take place both in a motel and in a hospital, open the door to a reckless, almost insensitive, comedic treatment.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Still, even with so many characters and subplots, the center of the story truly mirrors the journey of Olive, the Hoovers' naive and adorable daughter; the absolute soul of a gracefully revitalizing film. Young as she is, Abigail Breslin (b. 1996) wins over the audience playing a little girl who, though prone to insecurity, manages to overcome her fears, which are as powerful to her mind as adult fears are to the minds of grown-ups. The difference is that, while most adults prolong their own ordeals, Olive finds the key to getting past her fears and, on top of that, to getting past the worst nightmares of her loved ones. Even if it takes a few questionable routes, Little Miss Sunshine, a top-tier feel-good movie, is deeply surprising, bringing a spectacular cast, a committed screenplay, an emotional score and proficient direction. In the girl's mission to become Little Miss Sunshine, the family members redeem themselves, not by solving their problems, but by finding peace in the people with whom they will walk through the sea of challenges life brings. Victory, after all, lies not in the absence of defeat, but in the resolve to stand firm in the face of obstacles, which, even when they knock us down, need not necessarily crush hope, which, through thick and thin, will always remain.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Throughout his career, the director-actor-screenwriter Orson Welles (1915-1985) clashed with the studios in a struggle for control, seeking a way to complete his vision. The situation is no different in today's Hollywood, and successful directors such as the Coen brothers insist on having the final say over the editing of their work, ensuring that their films stand apart from Hollywood conventions. The challenge for American independent filmmakers is to offer audiences genuine alternatives to the themes and practices of standard Hollywood production.

segments.original: Indeed, independent films can be box-office hits: Little Miss Sunshine (2006) and Paranormal Activity (2007), a horror film with a microscopic budget, are recent examples. Another is Catfish (2010), which became famous on the back of a controversy over its supposedly documentary nature.

segments.original: Since the turn of the 21st century, the health of American independent cinema has drained away noticeably, but as equipment costs fall, the internet market grows and Hollywood's creativity stagnates, a resurgence of independent production should not be ruled out.
